clinicalPearls: Carcinoid heart disease is a complication of the carcinoid syndrome caused by vasoactive substances, particularly serotonin, released by metastatic neuroendocrine tumours
It characteristically affects the right-sided heart valves, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis or regurgitation with fibrous plaque-like thickening of the endocardium
Left-sided valve involvement is uncommon because the lungs inactivate circulating serotonin, but it can occur with a patent foramen ovale or bronchial carcinoid
It usually develops in patients with liver metastases, since hepatic clearance of tumour products is then bypassed
Right heart failure with peripheral oedema, ascites, and elevated venous pressure is the typical late presentation
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid and echocardiography are central to diagnosis, and elevated NT-proBNP supports cardiac involvement
Somatostatin analogues control syndrome symptoms and tumour secretion, while significant valve disease may require surgical valve replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Metastatic neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours, typically of midgut origin with hepatic metastases, secrete serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation. These substances stimulate fibroblast proliferation and deposition of fibrous tissue on the endocardium and valve leaflets, predominantly on the right side of the heart. The resulting plaque-like fibrosis retracts and immobilises the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, causing regurgitation and stenosis that lead to volume overload and right ventricular failure. Pulmonary inactivation of serotonin largely protects the left heart.
additionalDifferentials: Right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale
Ebstein anomaly or other congenital tricuspid disease
Drug-induced valvulopathy (for example from serotonergic agents)
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to characterise valve involvement and right ventricular function
Serum chromogranin A as a neuroendocrine tumour marker
NT-proBNP as a marker of cardiac involvement and severity
Cross-sectional and functional imaging (including somatostatin receptor imaging) to localise and stage the tumour
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure with ascites and oedema
Carcinoid crisis with flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, especially around procedures
Severe symptomatic valve dysfunction requiring surgical evaluation
Rapidly rising cardiac biomarkers indicating advancing cardiac disease
reference.prognosis: Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of survival in carcinoid syndrome and historically indicated advanced disease with a poor outlook, but somatostatin analogue therapy, tumour-directed treatment, and timely valve surgery have improved outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing right heart failure to more common causes and missing an underlying neuroendocrine tumour
Not screening for cardiac involvement in patients with established carcinoid syndrome
Failing to prevent and treat carcinoid crisis around surgery and interventions
Delaying valve surgery until right ventricular function is irreversibly impaired
